OBJECTIVE 1.1 Development Objective Original Development Objective (Approved as part of Approval package on 13-Dec-2016) The Project Development Objective (PDO) is to improve climate resilience and strengthen maintenance systems for a reliable road network in Lao PDR, and to provide immediate and effective response in case of an Eligible Crisis or Emergency. Has the Development Objective been changed since Board Approval of the Project Objective? Yes Current Development Objective (Approved as part of Additional Financing package Seq. 1 on 13-Dec-2019) The Project Development Objective (PDO) is to improve climate resilience and strengthen maintenance systems for a reliable road network in Lao PDR, and to provide immediate and effective response in case of an Eligible Crisis or Emergency. 2. KEY ISSUES & STATUS 4.1 Implementation Status and Key Decisions Progress towards achievement of the Project Development Objective (PDO) is on track, with all PDO indicators (6) having met the target. A total of 1,222 km of road receiving routine maintenance (PBC) has been completed in six project provinces. All 11 contracts (1,574.46 km) for the second three-year period (2023 – 2025) are under implementation, with physical progress at around 46-93%. For National Road 13 South (NR13S), roadworks has been under the operation and maintenance (O&M) phase. The Technical Assistance (TA) and institutional strengthening activities are almost completed. However, it is important to utilize the technical tools provided under the project (i.e., RMS, PRoMMS, IRAMS-2) to "modernize" MPWT's business process, especially with MPWT's staff shortage issue becoming more critical. There remains a need to address and improve on counterpart funding, overloading control, and road safety implementation. 5. KEY ISSUES & STATUS 4.1 Implementation Status and Key Decisions Progress towards achievement of the Project Development Objective (PDO) is on track, with all PDO indicators (6) having met the target. A total of 1,222 km of road receiving routine maintenance (PBC) has been completed in six project provinces. All 11 contracts (1,574 km) planned for the second three-year (2023 – 2025) PBC have been awarded and contractors mobilized with work progress at round 12 -74% completion. All sectoral planning tools developed and institutionalized, and it is now the time to focus on the utilization/piloting them. There remains a need to address and improve on counterpart funding, overloading control, and road safety implementation. 5. PROJECT CONTEXT AND DEVELOPMENT OBJECTIVES A. CONTEXT AT APPRAISAL CONTEXT 1. At appraisal in 2016, Lao PDR had sustained strong economic growth, averaging around 8 percent annually since 2000, driven by natural resources, infrastructure investment, and tourism. Although poverty had declined significantly, it remained concentrated in remote and ethnic minority areas. To support continued growth and rural development, the Government sought to improve regional and domestic connectivity as part of its strategy to transform Lao PDR from a landlocked to a land-linked economy. 2. Road transport was the backbone of the economy, carrying about 98 percent of passenger traffic and 96 percent of freight. However, the road network was increasingly affected by recurrent flooding and other climate-related events, which caused significant damage, expanded maintenance backlogs, and increased reliance on costly emergency repairs. Provincial and district roads were particularly vulnerable due to lower design standards, inadequate maintenance, and limited consideration of climate risks in infrastructure design. 3.

Fiscal constraints, inadequate road resilience, and weak maintenance capacity posed significant challenges to the sustainability of the road network. Frequent climate-related damage further strained limited resources and increased reconstruction, recovery and maintenance costs. Although road asset management systems had been established for both national and provincial roads —including the Road Management System (RMS) and the Provincial Road Maintenance Management System (PRoMMS), which were introduced progressively in the early to mid-2000s under earlier road sector programs—their effectiveness was constrained by weak data, limited integration of climate risk considerations, competing investment priorities, and capacity constraints at subnational levels. 4. To address these constraints and promote inclusive growth and economic diversification, the Government of Lao People’s Democratic Republic (GoL) sought financing from the World Bank for Lao Road Sector Project II (LRSP2) to improve resilience of road network, reduce recurring disaster recovery costs, and strengthen institutional capacity to maintain road reliability. The project was designed to anchor a broader sector-wide approach, with the World Bank serving as the lead financing and coordinating partner and the Nordic Development Fund (NFD) as co-financier.

LRSP2 intentionally leveraged financing for the European Investment Bank (EIB), the European Union (EU), and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), and Government road sector funding to enhance road network resilience, accessibility, and sustainability across the road sector as a whole within prioritized rural areas with high vulnerability to climate risks. To achieve these objectives, LRSP2 prioritized investment in disaster-prone rural areas in northern Lao PDR including Phongsaly, Houaphan, Oudomxay, Xiengkhouang, Xayabouly and Bolikhamxay provinces, where recurrent flash floods and slope failures frequently disrupted road connectivity. 5. LRSP2 built on the achievements of the Lao Road Sector Project (LRSP; P102398, 2010-2016). LRSP improved road conditions, established road asset management systems, strengthened road sector institutions, and enhanced rural connectivity (World Bank, 2022: 45)1. Expanding on these foundations, LRSP2 adopted a more systematic approach by integrating climate-resilient periodic maintenance into national and subnational road management systems and introducing a Contingency Emergency Response Component (CERC). The project also served as a platform for collaboration among development partners under the sector-wide approach, supporting harmonized investments and policy reforms across the road sector. LRSP2 was aligned with the World Bank’s Country Partnership Strategy for the 1 World Bank. 2022.

LRSP2 comprised four components to strengthen road maintenance systems at both the national and provincial/district levels, contributing to improved road reliability. LRSP2 was designed to mainstream best practices by implementing a sector-wide approach to addressing the full range of road maintenance challenges through the existing government institutional structure under the coordination of a Project Coordination Committee (PCC). Component 1 focused on enhancing maintenance systems at provincial and district levels, whereas Components 2 and 3 strengthened institutional capacities and project management functions across the entire road sector. By incorporating climate resilience as a cross-cutting element under Components 2 and 4, the project also helped the Government better prepare for—and respond to—potential road damage and service disruptions caused by climate-related disasters. In addition, the preparation of the CRRCIP provides a pathway to scale up maintenance practices, climate resilience standards, and asset management systems beyond LRSP2. V. LESSONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 77. The project showed that performance-based maintenance (PBC/OPBRC), supported by rolling multi-year maintenance planning and road asset management systems, can deliver and sustain improvements in road condition and accessibility when embedded in government decision-making and budget processes.

Integration of climate resilience into road maintenance systems in Lao PDR resulted from a sustained commitment to building institutional, technical, and human capital and institutionalizing maintenance systems among government stakeholders and Development Partners over the past decade. These results would not have been possible without strong and consistent government commitment, sustained engagement of the World Bank and other development partners, and strong task team leadership. 78. Climate resilience proved most effective when mainstreamed across the full maintenance cycle —from design and planning to asset management and execution—resulting in fewer disruptions, lower long-term costs, and more reliable connectivity. Development Partners coordination to promote PBC was a successful strategy to keep the road infrastructure sustainability in the climate vulnerable context of Lao PDR. Rewarding the contractors for regular and timely maintenance ensured maintenance completed which improved the resilience of the road network. Early agreement on common standards, aligned schedules, and a clear coordination framework were essential to fully realize the benefits to rolling out performance-based contracting in the context of parallel financing. 14 The World Bank Lao Road Sector Project 2 (LRSP2) (P158504) ICR DOCUMENT 79. The project also highlights that formal emergency response mechanisms such as CERC may not always be the preferred option for governments.

In practice, the ability to respond effectively depended more on operational readiness, including pre-agreed procedures under the ERM and the use of existing contract arrangements. Project restructuring and additional financing provided flexible and timely alternatives for mobilizing resources, enabling rapid restoration of connectivity without activating CERC. 15 The World Bank Lao Road Sector Project 2 (LRSP2) (P158504) ICR DOCUMENT ANNEX 1. EFFICIENCY ANALYSIS 1. The efficiency analysis for the ICR of the project is based on a cost-benefit analysis (CBA) approach, which follows the same methodology at appraisal stage, including additional financing stage.

The efficiency analysis covers the time horizon of 10 years (2017-2027) for road improvements and maintenance under the original project (Component 1.1 & 1.2) and 20 years (2019-2039) for the OPBRC under Additional Financing (Component 1.5), which are based on the life cycle of actual sub-projects implemented which are road improvement. The project supported the rehabilitation of 64 km of National Road 13 North. The key assumptions include: (i) the discount rate of 12 percent; (ii) the Standard Conversion Factor (SCF) of 0.92 for investment and 0.87 for maintenance; (iii) the project could help avoid some of the emergency maintenance due to the climate resiliency improvement; and (iv) the speed improvement from 47 km/h to 70 km/h on National Roads. 2. At appraisal, the economic internal rate of return (EIRR) for Components 1.1 and 1.2 (local road improvement and maintenance) was estimated at 31.5 percent, with a net present value (NPV) of US$6.85 million. Ex-post analysis conducted in 2026 indicates an EIRR of 31.5 percent and an NPV of US$19.95 million, suggesting that economic returns for local roads were broadly maintained, with higher realized benefits reflected in the increased NPV. 3. For the full 275 km NR13 South corridor, the ex-ante economic analysis conducted under the 2019 Additional Financing estimated an overall EIRR of 26.1 percent and an NPV of US$105.54 million.

At appraisal, the corridor was structured into three sections for analytical purposes, broadly reflecting the parallel financing arrangement across development partners, though not all sections were explicitly assigned to specific financiers. During implementation, the packaging of works was restructured from three into four sections to reflect contractor capacity and facilitate timely delivery, resulting in revised section boundaries and a clearer allocation of financing among IDA, EIB, and AIIB. Ex-post results indicate an EIRR of 34.4 percent and an NPV of US$37.8 million for Section 1 (approximately 40 km) financed under the IDA credit, compared to an overall EIRR of 33.9 percent and an NPV of US$212.46 million for the full NR13S corridor. 4. This distinction reflects the underlying financing structure. While IDA financing supported Section 1 of NR13S, the economic benefits of rehabilitating and operating the full corridor were realized at the aggregate level through coordinated multi-partner implementation. Accordingly, economic efficiency can be assessed both at the level of IDA‑financed investments and at the level of overall corridor outcomes achieved through coordinated multi‑partner implementation. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS Borrower’s Comments LRSP2 has been a priority project for the Government of the Lao PDR. The project supported a critical period of transition for the road sector from reactive, emergency-driven maintenance practices toward a systematic, data-informed, and climate-resilient approach to road asset management. The investments made under LRSP2 have directly strengthened the capacity of MPWT and its provincial departments (DPWTs) to plan, finance, and deliver road maintenance more effectively and sustainably.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: MPWT is particularly pleased with the institutionalization of the three-year rolling climate-resilient road maintenance planning process, which is now embedded in the government's annual budget preparation cycle. This reform represents a fundamental shift in how the Ministry approaches road asset management and reflects a long-term commitment to ensuring that Lao PDR's road network can withstand the growing impacts of climate change. The use of risk-informed planning tools, including the Integrated Road Asset Management System (IRAMS-2), the Road Management System (RMS), and the Provincial Road Maintenance Management System (PRoMMS) has given MPWT the institutional foundation to prioritize investments based on evidence rather than on an ad-hoc basis. The project's introduction of OPBRC on National Road 13 South contributes to the landmark achievement for the road sector in Lao PDR. NR13 South is a critical national corridor, and the OPBRC model has demonstrated that private sector pre-financing can be effectively mobilized to deliver climate-resilient rehabilitation and long-term maintenance under a single integrated contract. This modality reduces the immediate fiscal burden on government while aligning the contractor's incentives with road condition outcomes rather than volume of inputs.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: Based on the success of this pilot on NR13 South under LRSP2, MPWT is committed to expanding the OPBRC approach to other priority national roads, including the ongoing NR13 North project and future operations. MPWT extends its sincere gratitude to the World Bank, the principal financier, and to the Nordic Development Fund (NDF) for their co-financing and parallel financing contributions. The Ministry acknowledges the active and consistent support provided by both partners throughout all phases of project preparation and implementation. This included technical assistance in procurement, design, and supervision; support to the development of performance-based contracting methodologies and standard bidding documents; guidance on climate resilience mainstreaming; training for MPWT and DPWT staff in PBC and OPBRC implementation, road safety audits, and environmental and social (E&S) safeguards; and close monitoring of contract implementation and safeguard compliance. This engagement was essential to the project's success and has left lasting benefits in the form of enhanced institutional capacity across the sector. MPWT also recognizes the important contribution of the NDF to the climate resilience dimensions of the project, particularly in financing climate-resilient periodic maintenance and spot improvements and the establishment of vulnerability mapping and risk-based planning tools under the RAMS/PRoMMS system.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: This support was instrumental in shifting the Ministry's planning culture from reactive emergency response to predictive, risk-informed asset management a transformation that will generate lasting dividends for the reliability and resilience of the national road network. MPWT also wishes to express its appreciation to the EIB and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) for their Page 33 Official Use Only The World Bank Lao Road Sector Project 2 (LRSP2) (P158504) ICR DOCUMENT parallel financing of sections of National Road 13 South. The participation of EIB and AIIB provided the additional scale necessary to address the full length of this critical corridor under a harmonized, performance-based contracting framework. Their adoption of the World Bank's OPBRC standards and common technical specifications ensured consistency in quality and climate resilience requirements across all sections of NR13 South, regardless of the financing source. This coordinated multi-financier approach set a strong precedent for development partner collaboration in Lao PDR's road sector, and MPWT looks forward to continued engagement with EIB and AIIB in future infrastructure initiatives.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: The Ministry acknowledges that challenges were encountered during implementation, including macroeconomic pressures, particularly the sharp depreciation of the Lao Kip and inflationary trends, which reduced the real value of Road Fund counterpart financing and constrained the scope of routine maintenance deliverable under Component 1. The Ministry is committed to addressing these fiscal challenges going forward by strengthening RMF revenues, exploring supplementary financing mechanisms including potential tolling on key corridors, and continuing to advocate for adequate budget allocations for road maintenance within the national budget framework. The integration of road asset management priorities into the draft Transport Sector Five-Year Plan (2026–2030) reflects the government's commitment to sustaining and building upon the reforms introduced under LRSP2. MPWT also recognizes the progress made on road safety under LRSP2, including the approval by the Prime Minister's Office of the National Road Safety Strategy and Action Plan (2021–2030) and Action Plan (2021–2025). The Ministry will continue to pursue the implementation of this strategy and calls on development partners to sustain their engagement on road safety as a critical cross-cutting priority for the sector. Finally, MPWT wishes to acknowledge the dedication of the Project Management Unit (PMU) and all DoR and DPWT staff who contributed to the implementation of LRSP2.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: Their efforts, alongside those of the World Bank and NDF teams, have delivered results well above original targets on direct beneficiaries, the rural population with access to an all-season road, and share of women in project-related paid employment. These results reflect the project's contribution not only to road connectivity but also to the broader development and inclusion goals of the government. Page 34 Official Use Only

Procurement Plan A. GENERAL 1. Project Information: - Country: Lao PDR - Borrower/Recipient: Lao PDR - Project Name: Lao Road Sector Project 2 (LRSP 2) – Additional Finance - Project Number: P158504 - Project Implementation Agency: Ministry of Public Works and Transport Department of Finance (DoF) will take overall responsibility for procurement management. Each procurement package will be conducted by Department and DPWT concern including: Department of Roads (DOR), Department of Transport (DOT), Public Works and Transport Research Institute (PTRI), Public Works and Transport Training Institute (PTTI), Department of Personnel (DoP), Department of Inspection (DOI) and Cabinet Office in Ministry of Public Works & Transport (MPWT) and Department of Public Works & Transport (DPWTs) in the provinces. 2. Date of the Procurement Plan: • November 2022 3. Period covered by this Procurement Plan: 30 months (from the effectiveness date) B. PREAMBLE In accordance with paragraph 5.9 of the “World Bank Procurement Regulations for IPF Borrowers” (Jul. 2016) (“Procurement Regulations”) the Bank’s Systematic Tracking and Exchanges in Procurement (STEP) system will be used to prepare, clear and update Procurement Plans and conduct all procurement transactions for the Project. This textual part along with the Procurement Plan tables in STEP constitute the Procurement Plan for the Project. The following conditions apply to all procurement activities in the Procurement Plan.

The other elements of the Procurement Plan as required under paragraph 4.4 of the Procurement Regulations are set forth in STEP. The Bank’s Standard Procurement Documents: shall be used for all contracts subject to international competitive procurement and those contracts as specified in the Procurement Plan tables in STEP. National Procurement Arrangements: In accordance with paragraph 5.3 of the Procurement Regulations, when approaching the national market (as specified in the Procurement Plan tables in STEP), the country’s own procurement procedures may be used. When the Borrower uses its own national open competitive procurement arrangements as set forth in the Public Procurement Law No. 30/NA, dated 2 Nov. 2017 and the Instruction on Implementation Public Procurement Law No.

0477/MOF, dated 13 February 2019, such arrangements shall be subject to paragraph 5.4 of the Procurement Regulations and the following conditions: a) The request for bids/request for proposals document shall require that bidders/proposers submitting bids/proposals present a signed acceptance at the time of bidding, to be incorporated in any resulting contracts, confirming application of, and compliance with, Bank Anti-Corruption Guidelines, including without limitation the Bank’s right to sanction and the Bank’s inspection and audit rights; b) Information related to award of contract including reasons for rejection of unsuccessful bidders shall be published on the implementing agency websites and/or newspaper of wide circulation. c) All complaints on procurement related matters including complaints arising from procurement under Bank financed Projects whilst using National Procurement Procedures shall be dealt with in accordance with Article 33 of the Procurement Decree. Borrower shall put in place an effective complaint review mechanism for dealing with procurement related complaints and shall disclose the details in all the bidding documents. All complaints shall be recorded by the Borrower in the appropriate tracking and monitoring system, as agreed between the Bank and the Borrower.

When other national procurement arrangements other than national open competitive procurement arrangements are applied by the Borrower, such arrangements shall be subject to paragraph 5.5 of the Procurement Regulations. Leased Assets as specified under paragraph 5.10 of the Procurement Regulations: Leasing may be used for those contracts identified in the Procurement Plan tables. Not Applicable. Procurement of Second-Hand Goods as specified under paragraph 5.11 of the Procurement Regulations - is allowed for those contracts identified in the Procurement Plan tables. Not Applicable. Domestic preference as specified under paragraph 5.51 of the Procurement Regulations (Goods and Works). - Goods: is applicable for those contracts identified in the Procurement Plan tables; - Works: is applicable for those contracts identified in the Procurement Plan tables. Sub-project Procurement Plan will be prepared separately each year and sent to the World Bank for information and reference. All activities under sub-projects will be subjected to the World Bank’s post review and will not be posted on the STEP. C. OTHER RELEVANT PROCUREMENT INFORMATION I.
